text: Slow recruitment in a red-fox population following poison baiting: a non-invasive mark–recapture analysis

Context. Optimal management of invasive species should determine the interval between lethal-control operations that will sustain a desired population suppression at minimum cost. This requires an understanding of the species' rate of recruitment following control. These data are difficult to acquire for vertebrate carnivores such as the red fox (Vulpes vulpes), which are not readily trapped or observed.Aims. To provide a long-term evaluation of the effects of 1080 poison baiting on the abundance and extent of movement of red foxes in a semiarid environment.Methods. We used non-invasive DNA sampling of fox hairs in semi-arid Western Australia where the population was subject to two episodes of aerially delivered sodium fluoroacetate (1080) poison baits within 12 months. Sampling took place at ~45-day intervals and individual foxes were identified by genotyping eight microsatellite DNA markers and a genderspecific marker. Open-population and spatially explicit mark-recapture models were used to estimate the density, apparent survival and movements of foxes before and following baiting.Key results. Following a severe reduction in density after baiting, fox density during the ensuing 12 months increased slowly (0.01 foxes km -2 month -1 ), such that density had only reached 22% of pre-baiting levels ~10 months after the initial baiting. Moreover, recovery was non-linear as population growth was negligible for 6 months, then exhibited a nine-fold increase 7-9 months after control, coincident with the dispersal of juveniles in autumn. Fox movements between recaptures were on average 470% greater after baiting than before, in line with expectations for low-density populations, suggesting that the probability of encountering baits during this period would be higher than before baiting.Conclusions. Baiting with 1080 poison significantly reduced the density of foxes, and the low density was sustained for more than 6 months. Foxes moved significantly further between recaptures after baiting when at low densities.Implications. Control programs in this region may be carried out at low frequency to suppress fox density to a fraction of unbaited levels. The intensity of follow-up baiting may also be adjusted downwards, to take account of an increased probability of bait encounter in more mobile foxes.

Details on the study site have been presented elsewhere (see Berry et al. 2012), and a brief summary is presented here. The study was carried out at Karara and Lochada pastoral stations, Western Australia (28 58 0 05 00 S, 116 40 0 51 00 E), which are adjacent reclaimed pastoral leases. The landscape is semiarid (rainfall 320 mm annually) and is dominated by mixed Acacia shrublands and sparse York gum (Eucalyptus loxophleba) woodlands. Minimal predator control had been conducted on the pastoral leases and the surrounding area before the present study and mostly by neighbouring pastoral leases in an ad hoc manner, to control wild dogs (Canis familiaris).

We employed eight transects, each containing 11 'sticky wicket' hair-snares spaced at 1-km intervals. The 'sticky wicket' trapped hair as foxes passed between three vertical sticks covered in double-sided tape to enter a monitoring plot containing scent and audio lures (Berry et al. 2012). We employed a mixture of linear and irregularly shaped transects that encompassed 90degree bends. By necessity, transects ran along dirt tracks and hair-snares were placed adjacent and running perpendicular to the tracks within the shrubland vegetation. Although the tracks were predominantly cleared of vegetation, in general, the dominant shrubland vegetation at Karara-Lochada is open enough that foxes can travel unimpeded. We, therefore, assumed that the placement of hair-snares in the vicinity of the tracks minimally biased our analysis. Furthermore, the even density of tracks throughout Karara-Lochada (Fig. 1) should mean that our analysis was representative of the study area. The present study incorporated capture information from the final two sessions reported previously (Berry et al. 2012), namely June and August 2008, here identified as Sessions 1 and 2, and extended an identical sampling regime of ~45-day intervals between sampling sessions that each consisted of four consecutive sampling days (occasions) for a further 12 months until July 2009 (six further sessions). The final sampling session in July 2009 occurred 20 days after deployment from an aircraft of 1080 poison baits at 50 baits km -2 , which was identical to the deployment implemented in August 2008 (Berry et al. 2012), and covered the entire Karara-Lochada study site and a further 5-km buffer from the property boundary. Fifty baits km -2 is the operational rate for feral-cat control (Algar and Burrows 2004). A large rainfall event followed several days after the September 2008 baiting, making it unlikely that baits remained viable for long after. In total, eight sampling sessions took place; however, samples were not obtained for three of these sessions because foxes were absent or at extremely low densities and hairs were not collected on hair-snares.
Sticky wickets were checked daily and hairs were removed from the tape with sterilised forceps, placed in a sealed paper envelope, labelled, frozen at À20 C and transported to the DNA laboratory within 2 weeks of collection. To limit any effect of time on the quality and quantity of DNA in each follicle, DNA extraction was carried out within 2 weeks of the receipt of the samples. Laboratory analyses were conducted under strict protocols and guidelines, to minimise poor-quality samples and reduce genotyping errors (see Berry et al. (2012). DNA was extracted from a maximum of 10 hairs per sample (minimum 1; mean 3.8 AE 0.2) by using the Qiagen DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit (Cat. 69504; Hilden, Germany).

Following DNA extraction, samples were genotyped with eight microsatellite DNA loci and the gender of each fox was determined with a male-specific sry product (Berry et al. 2012). Three PCR replicates of each locus were made for each sample. Results of the fragment analysis were analysed using GENEMARKER (SoftGenetics, State College, PA, USA) and all allele calling was checked by eye. The male-specific marker amplified only in the presence of male fox DNA. Therefore, to distinguish between a female and failed amplification, each sample without sry amplification was cross-referenced, with the amplification success of two microsatellite loci coamplified in the PCR multiplex (Berry et al. 2012).
Consensus genotypes were calculated according to the criterion of Frantz et al. (2003) where a homozygous genotype was accepted if the same single allele was present in all three replicates, and a heterozygous genotype was accepted if two different alleles were present in each of two or more replicates. Consensus genotypes for each sample were input into the Excel macro GENECAP (Wilberg and Dreher 2004), which identified genotypes differing by one or two alleles, generated capture histories, provided allele frequencies and probability of identity (PID) statistics (Waits et al. 2001). On the basis of PID results presented in Berry et al. (2012), samples that produced consensus genotypes at five or more loci were sufficiently informative to distinguish individuals and were used to create capture histories. Samples that did not meet the criteria were re-amplified and re-genotyped to obtain more complete genotypes (one example in each of Sessions 1 and 2). Allelic dropout (ADO) and false alleles (FA) were computed from the data with the program GIMLET (Valiere 2002). Identifying individual foxes in this manner is analogous to direct capture for the purposes of capture-recapture analysis.

section: density estimation using spatially explicit capture-recapture (secr) models
text: Spatially explicit capture-recapture (SECR) models generated in the program DENSITY were used to estimate the density of foxes within Sessions 1, 6 and 7 (Efford 2004;Efford et al. 2009). SECR uses the locations that each animal is captured to fit a model of the detection process and to provide an estimate of density that is unbiased by incomplete detection and edge effects (Efford 2004). We used the full maximum likelihood estimator (Borchers and Efford 2008) of density (D), and a halfnormal detection function incorporating g 0 (susceptibility to capture at the centre of a home range), and s (a measure of the spatial extent of susceptibility to capture). We identified our hair-snares as proximity detectors (allowing multiple withinoccasion captures per individual), and ran the analysis with a buffer of 10 000 m. Alternative buffer sizes and detection functions had a minimal effect on parameter estimates. Sixteen biologically plausible models were fitted to the capture data and their fit was evaluated with Akaike's information criterion corrected for a small sample size (AICc; Burnham and Anderson 2002). We tested models that maintained a constant density throughout the sampling period, D(.), or a change in density between sessions, D(session). Models that allowed for behavioural responses to capture (b), and individual heterogeneity (two-group mixture; h), in both g 0 and s, and all combinations of these variables, were also tested. Parameters were estimated with model averaging. Sessions 2, 3, 4, 5 and 8 were excluded from the SECR analyses because, at most, one sample was collected in any of those sessions. However, an approximate density was calculated for Sessions 2 and 5 when a single fox was captured by dividing one by the mean effective sampling area identified with SECR modelling during three pre-baiting sessions (Berry et al. 2012;293.3 km 2 ). Sex was not included in the models because of low sample sizes.

Open-population capture-recapture analysis, based on Pollock's robust design, was conducted with the program MARK (White and Burnham 1999). This analysis enabled estimation of apparent survival (s), capture probability (p), recapture probability (c), abundance ( N ) and temporary immigration (G). Four biologically plausible models were constructed that included behavioural responses to capture (probability of recapture = probability of capture) and individual heterogeneity in capture (two-group mixture). Models that incorporated change in survival and abundance between sessions were also considered, as were models that kept these parameters constant. This analysis was applied to all sessions where foxes were detected (i.e. excluding Sessions 3, 4 and 8). The support for competing models was ranked with AICc, and parameters were estimated with model averaging.

The mean distance moved by individual foxes between recaptures was calculated as the cumulative distance moved between trapping locations in order of recapture date within a session, divided by the number of recaptures. Individuals never recaptured were not included in these analyses. For this analysis, we included movement information from foxes collected under comparable experimental conditions during pre-baiting Sessions 1-3 described in Berry et al. (2012). Data were checked for homogeneity of variances with Cochran's C test. Data with heterogeneous variances were log-transformed. A Student's t-test comparing the log10 mean distance moved before and after 1080 baiting (Sessions 2-7) was conducted with the software package JMP (version 5.0; SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA).

section: species identification, genotyping and error rates
text:
Thirty-five hair samples were collected during Sessions 3-8. These were added to the 52 samples collected from Sessions 1 and 2 that represented 24 individual foxes (Berry et al. 2012).
Thirty-four of the 35 samples were identified as fox, and of these, 33 (97%) provided more than five locus microsatellite genotypes (6 locus n = 2, 8 locus n = 31; Table S1, available as Supplementary Material for this paper). Including the samples from Sessions 1 and 2, 60, 21 and four samples provided eight, seven and six locus genotypes, respectively (no five locus genotypes). No samples contained more than two alleles at any loci, indicating that there were no instances of mixed samples.
Comparisons of genotypes revealed no cases of one-and twoallele mismatches. The average per locus, per replicate rate of allelic dropout (ADO) was 0.016, and the average per locus, per replicate rate of false alleles (FA) was 0.014. The probability of identity (sibling) for the most variable five loci was 0.006, and for the five least variable loci was 0.012, indicating that the fivelocus criterion for accepting genotypes was acceptable. The probability of identity (unrelated) for both the most and least variable five loci was <0.001. Among samples identified as recaptures, the mean probability that any pair of samples were full siblings rather than true recaptures (PIDsib) was 0.003 (AE0.0002 s.e.) and the maximum PIDsib between any pair of samples was 0.012, with only one instance of >0.01

Five samples (15%) collected during Sessions 3-8 yielded unique genotypes, and thus represented individual foxes. Twenty-eight samples (85%) yielded genotypes that were present at least twice in the dataset and represented six different individuals. In total, 11 individual foxes (seven males and four females) were identified during Sessions 2-7. The initial pre-baiting (Session 1) sex ratio of male:female was 1 : 1.3 (n = 23) and post-baiting (Sessions 2-8) was 1.75 : 1 (n = 11).
The sex ratio pre and post-baiting was not significantly different (c 2 with Yates correction = 0.54, P = 0.46). None of the 23 foxes caught in the session before baiting was recaptured in any of the seven sessions following baiting.

Density was estimated directly for Sessions 1, 6 and 7, when multiple individual foxes were detected. All well supported models incorporated a session effect on density and the spatial extent of susceptibility to capture (s) (Table 1). The best supported model also included a behavioural response to capture (probability of capture = probability of recapture), and heterogeneity in response to capture g 0 (b + h). Models ranked 2 and 3 also included heterogeneity in s. The parameter estimates for Session 1 differ slightly from those from the same session (labelled Session 3) in Berry et al. (2012) because of differences in the models selected by AICc and the incorporation of data from different sessions.
Fox density decreased substantially following the initial 1080 baiting, from an estimate of 0.51 foxes km -2 (AE0.17 s.e.) to 0.003 foxes km -2 . Over the following 12 months (7 sessions) density remained very low and not estimatable by SECR, until Sessions 6 and 7 when it increased to a maximum of 0.11 foxes km -2 AE 0.04 s.e. just before the second episode of aerial baiting (Fig. 2), after which no foxes were detected in Session 8. The probability of capture at the centre of a home range g 0 was 0.160 (AE0.092 s.e.) and 0.007 (AE0.014 s.e.) for the 'trap happy' and 'trap shy' groups, respectively.

The best supported model incorporated change in abundance and apparent survival between sessions and assumed unequal probability of capture and recapture (Table 2). Temporary emigration was constant in these models. Model averaging indicated that there were 30.75 trappable foxes (AE6.83 s.e.) present at Karara-Lochada during Session 1 before the initial baiting and 3.23 (AE0.079 s.e.) in Session 2 immediately after baiting and also in Session 5 (Fig. 3). Ten months after baiting, the number of trappable foxes present in the study area had risen to 12.94 (AE4.09 s.e.) by Session 7. The model-averaged probability of capture was 0.20 (AE0.07 s.e.), and probability of recapture was 0.23 (AE0.04 s.e.). Apparent survival following the initial 1080 baiting (between Sessions 1 and 2) was effectively zero, and remained zero (inestimable) for ~7 months because of zero or sparse captures until the period between Sessions 6 and 7, where it rose to 0.68, which is similar to that before baiting (Berry et al. 2012), although the analysis could not resolve standard error for this estimate because of limited sample size.

section: changes in the extent of movement between recaptures
text: Foxes moved significantly further between recaptures after baiting than they did before baiting (Fig. 4; t = 3.41, d.f. = 18, Table 1. P < 0.001). Individual foxes did not move between transects in the pre-baiting session, but three foxes moved between transects following baiting, with two of these foxes (both male) moving over 10 km in one day. The parameter s, which describes the spatial extent in susceptibility of capture, and thus indexes home-range size (Efford 2004), was 629.01 m (AE119.52 s.e.) in Session 1 before baiting. During Sessions 6 and 7 (when captures were sufficient to estimate s), it increased to 5174.74 m (AE1078.26 s.e.) and 2600.64 m (AE834.62 s.e.), respectively (values from the best supported model).
